items.q: An IoT 'sense → analyse → act' loop breaks if analytics is removed because:
options: Collected data remains raw and unactionable — no insight is produced to drive decisions
items.explain: Without analytics, sensor data is just raw, unstructured noise. Analytics is the pillar that converts data into the insight that closes the loop into action.

items.q: The original motivation behind Kevin Ashton's 'Internet of Things' was that computers of the era:
options: Knew only what humans manually entered, so giving objects (via RFID) the ability to gather their own data would cut waste and cost
Could not connect to the internet at all
items.explain: Ashton's insight: if objects could capture their own data automatically (RFID), systems could track everything without error-prone human data entry — reducing waste and cost.

items.q: A factory wants very high data rate and very high reliability for a fixed, mains-powered control system. Which connectivity is most appropriate?
items.explain: For a static, powered, critical industrial system needing very high throughput and reliability, wired Ethernet is the natural choice (power and short range are non-issues).

items.q: Match the gateway function to its description: 'collects data from many devices and sends it upstream efficiently' is:
items.explain: Data aggregation gathers many devices' data and forwards it as fewer, larger, efficient transmissions — distinct from protocol translation (format conversion) and bridging (non-IP↔IP).

items.q: Which architectural response is NOT primarily a scalability mechanism?
options: Message queuing/streaming (MQTT, Kafka) to decouple producers and consumers
items.explain: Encryption (DTLS/TLS) is a security mechanism. Microservices, message queues, and horizontal scaling are the standard architectural answers to the scalability driver.

items.q: The delay between a controller issuing a command and the physical action occurring is which type of latency?
items.explain: Actuation latency is the lag from command issuance to physical actuation. Network latency is travel time; processing latency is analysis time; end-to-end is the total.

items.q: In the 5-layer model, the layer often called the 'cognition' or 'brain' layer — performing filtering, aggregation, and decision-making — is the:
items.explain: The data-processing/middleware layer is the 'brain' — filtering, aggregating, contextual processing, and triggering decisions, often hosting edge/fog nodes.

items.q: In the canonical Cisco IoTWF 7-layer model, which layer is responsible for converting data 'in motion' (streams) into data 'at rest' (storage)?
items.explain: Data Accumulation (Layer 4) stores streaming data so non-real-time applications can query it. Data Abstraction (Layer 5) then reconciles/normalises it for apps.

items.q: Place these IoTWF layers in bottom-to-top order: Application, Physical Devices & Controllers, Data Abstraction, Connectivity, Data Accumulation, Edge Computing, Collaboration & Processes.
options: Physical Devices → Connectivity → Edge Computing → Data Accumulation → Data Abstraction → Application → Collaboration & Processes
Application → Physical Devices → Connectivity → Edge Computing → Data Abstraction → Data Accumulation → Collaboration & Processes
Connectivity → Physical Devices → Application → Edge Computing → Data Accumulation → Data Abstraction → Collaboration & Processes
Physical Devices → Edge Computing → Connectivity → Application → Data Abstraction → Data Accumulation → Collaboration & Processes
items.explain: Data rises and refines: devices (1) → connectivity (2) → edge computing (3) → data accumulation (4) → data abstraction (5) → application (6) → collaboration & processes (7).

items.q: Which Communications-Network sublayer carries application-messaging protocols such as CoAP and MQTT between head-end apps and sensors?
items.explain: The IoT network management sublayer adds application-messaging protocols (CoAP, MQTT). Network transport handles IP/UDP; the access network is the last physical hop.

items.q: Classifying a smart object as 'battery-powered, mobile, low reporting frequency, simple data, long range' most strongly suggests which connectivity family?
items.explain: Battery + mobile + low-frequency + simple data + long range is the LPWAN profile — exactly what LoRaWAN/NB-IoT are optimised for.

items.q: Which statement about the edge–fog–cloud hierarchy is FALSE?
options: Edge offers the lowest latency and can operate during network disruption
Fog sits at the LAN level, aggregating data from multiple edge devices
Cloud provides massive scalability and advanced AI/ML analytics
Real systems must pick exactly one tier and never combine them
items.explain: Real systems are hybrid — edge for reflexes, fog for site coordination, cloud for heavy analytics. The skill is placing each function at the right tier, not choosing only one.

items.q: A key reason oneM2M is described as a 'horizontal' architecture is that:
options: It only works for smart homes
Its common service layer (CSE) is reused across many verticals instead of each industry building its own silo
It requires vertical scaling of servers
It runs exclusively on the device
items.explain: oneM2M defines one standardised service layer shared by all verticals, avoiding per-industry silos and vendor lock-in — the essence of a horizontal architecture.

items.q: Along the IoT value chain (silicon → device → connectivity → platform → analytics → service), value and margin tend to concentrate:
options: At the silicon/hardware end, furthest from the customer
Toward the analytics/service end, closest to the customer's actual problem
items.explain: Raw sensor data is nearly worthless; value accrues as data is connected, stored, analysed, and packaged into outcomes — so margins concentrate toward the service end (services over hardware).

items.q: Which standards body is correctly paired with its IoT contribution?
items.explain: IETF defines internet protocols for constrained devices (CoAP, 6LoWPAN, RPL). 3GPP does cellular (NB-IoT/LTE-M/5G); IEEE does 802.11/802.15.4 radios; oneM2M is the service layer.

items.q: What is the most common non-technical reason IoT projects fail?
options: Starting from the technology instead of a measurable use case and KPI
items.explain: Projects that begin with 'sensors looking for a problem' — no defined use case or KPI — drown in data-overload and cost. Start from the business goal and metric.

items.q: Why are the major IoT challenges described as 'interlocking' rather than independent?
options: Fixing one often pressures another — e.g., tight power budgets push devices to skimp on encryption (security) and send less data (reliability)
They only occur in smart homes
They disappear once devices scale up
items.explain: Power limits force weaker crypto and sparser data; device scale worsens the data deluge; missing standards complicate securing and scaling — the challenges trade off against one another.

items.q: A self-driving deployment needs both instant local reactions and global fleet learning. The most realistic architecture is:
options: A hybrid edge + cloud (often with fog) — edge for reflexes, cloud for heavy learning
items.explain: Edge handles millisecond safety reactions and offline operation; the cloud aggregates fleet data for heavy ML. Most production IoT is hybrid, placing each function at the right tier.
